Enzyme Replacement Therapy

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Imagine learning your child has a rare, life-threatening, but treatable disease...and it's covered by medical aid...only to be turned down by your medical aid scheme.

Unique Selling Point:
Enzyme therapy is a new and stunningly expensive treatment for a small group of diseases that affect only a few people in the world. Treatment can cost hundreds of thousands per month - yet it is the only thing that can offer these people a chance at a normal life. And these diseases are Prescribed Minimum Benefits under the Medical Schemes Act, which means that medical aid schemes are obligated to cover the treatment. And yet in case after case, medical aids refuse, dragging patients and their families through lengthy hearings with the CMS which to date, have always resulted in a decision in the patient's favour. But patients will suffer permanent disease progression and damage - and in some cases, even death, while they wait.

Summary:
Rare diseases affect 4% of the world's population: cumulatively, a huge number of people. This is a story about a group of rare, genetic, metabolic diseases affecting around 90 known patients in South Africa. These diseases result in a deficiency of enzymes needed to process carbohydrates, proteins and fats, resulting in a build-up on organs, joints and muscles, leading to irreversible damage and eventually death. Life expectancy differs according to the type and severity of the disease, but is severely curtailed.

Many children aren't diagnosed until damage has occurred, thanks to the diseases' rarity. For those lucky enough to get an early diagnosis, the good news is that it's possible in some conditions to replace the deficient enzymes, which slows progression of the disease, increases life expectancy and allows the child to live normally. Even better: "Life-threatening congenital abnormalities of carbohydrate, lipid, protein and amino acid metabolism" appear on the list of Prescribed Minimum Benefits for which medical aids (and government) must provide treatment. The treatment is "medical management": the only available and effective version is enzyme replacement therapy.

But that's where the good news ends. Medical aid schemes refuse to approve the treatment, citing its "biological" or "experimental" nature, claiming they can't afford it, or saying the disease is not a PMB. Parents are forced to watch their child deteriorate, eventually being placed on a ventilator or hospitalised (for which medical aid pays) and dying.

Enter Rare Diseases South Africa. They've taken numerous schemes repeatedly to the Council for Medical Schemes and haven't lost a single case, forcing medical aid schemes to pay for treatment. And yet every new patient is forced to go through the same painful process, waiting up to three years and facing irreversible deterioration.

Further information:
Rare Diseases South Africa was founded by Kelly du Plessis, whose son Juan was fortuitously diagnosed with Pompe Disease at only 11 months. Most babies with Pompe don't live to see their second birthdays. Juan was the first South African child to receive enzyme replacement therapy covered by his medical aid, thanks to Kelly's fight for coverage. Today he is an energetic 13 year-old with completely normal cardiac function, thanks to his treatment of 12 years. He is the success story for enzyme replacement therapy - but sadly too few children will have the same chance. Having won her own battle, Kelly was inspired to fight for other families, and today Rare Diseases South Africa advocates for every patient with a rare disease free of charge. They have taken numerous cases of metabolic storage disorders to the CMS and have never lost. Despite creating a precedent for the coverage of these diseases by medical aid schemes, however, they continue to see many children delayed and permanently damaged thanks to the schemes' refusal.

OTHER CASE STUDIES
Zachary de Wet is a three year old with a shock of blond hair and a sweet smile. He was fortunately diagnosed with Mucopolysaccharidosis type II when he was about two years old, thanks to an alert doctor who recognised some of the symptoms. MPSII is the deficiency of a protein required to metabolise proteins, and these proteins then build up all over Zachary's body, including on his heart and other organs, his joints and his muscles. They can also cross the blood-brain barrier. Once a seemingly normal toddler, Zachary now shows some developmental delays in his speech and cognition, and two valves in his heart have started leaking. Although his family is on a medical aid, the scheme (MediHelp) has refused to pay for treatment. Facing the prospect of a long battle during which Zachary may lose his ability to walk and face permanent mental disability, the family has decided to take the scheme to court, hoping to set a legal precedent for other families.

Crishendo Bowers was a sweet, funny kid with a big smile, and MPSII. He received treatment for several years until his granny, who used to pay for his medical aid, passed away. Although his mom quickly found a job which included medical aid, the new scheme (Bankmed) refused to pay for his life-saving treatment. After a year-long battle, Crishendo passed away in 2021 from complications of the disease without ever receiving approval.

Mbali Mvubelo is a young woman who was diagnosed with Gaucher disease many years ago. She had a spleen so large that she was continuously shamed for being a pregnant teenager. She now receives treatment at Charlotte Maxeke hospital and is living a normal life now despite her condition. She has a disease for which treatment is fairly available in government, but others who have different forms of metabolic disease are less fortunate.

Extra Budget Items:
Additional shoot day with internal crew, probably in two halves:
1. Travel to Potchefstroom to pick up interview with medical expert.
2. Interview with legal expert at time and location TBC

Press Release:


Imagine learning your child has a rare, life-threatening, but treatable disease...and it's a condition covered by medical aid...only for your medical aid scheme to refuse funding for lifesaving treatment.

This is a story about a group of rare, genetic disorders resulting in a deficiency of the essential enzymes needed to process substances in our cells. The substances build up on organs, bones and muscles, leading to irreversible damage and eventually death. Enzyme Replacement Therapy replaces the deficient enzymes, slowing progression of the disease, increasing life expectancy, and often allowing the patient to live a normal life. But it is stunningly expensive: a single month’s supply can cost hundreds of thousands of rands. The good news for patients is that these diseases are Prescribed Minimum Benefits, which means that according to the Medical Schemes Act, medical aid schemes are obligated to cover treatment. And yet in case after case, medical aids refuse, dragging patients and their families through lengthy hearings with the Council for Medical Schemes. To date, the process has always resulted in a decision in the patient's favour. But patients will suffer permanent disease progression and damage - and in some cases, even death - while they wait.

We tell the emotional stories of families on the receiving end of this bitter conundrum as they battle to ensure a healthy future for their children.

Script:


UPSOUND: Juan du Plessis: Dad’s going to make a silly mistake and now I’m back in the game.
LINK: We’re here in Hartbeespoort on an ordinary Sunday, to visit a family as they go about their weekend routine. But ordinary life has not come easily for Kelly du Plessis and her son, Juan.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: So this is just our mixing process. It takes about two and a bit hours.
Masa: Two and a half hours!
Kelly: Ja. And then it takes another five and a half to 6 hours to actually infuse. So it's quite a commitment. This is our Sunday every second week, except I'm normally in pyjamas.
VO1: This is a story about lifesaving medical treatment - but it’s also a story about parents fighting to keep their children alive.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: This medicine keeps his heart functioning. It keeps him breathing. It keeps all of his muscle functioning properly. This stuff is like liquid gold for us. It's like liquid life.
VO2: Juan was very young when Kelly realised he was facing serious health problems.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: I think I knew from about the time he was ten days old, was the first time he had a significant choking episode. Other children were a lot more active than he was, and they were definitively reaching their gross motor milestones easier.
VO3: By the time Juan was 11 months old, he had a diagnosis. He has Pompe disease, one of a group of rare genetic diseases called lysosomal storage disorders.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: If you combine them, they have an incidence of around about one in 5000 to 1 in 6000 live births.
VO4: Professor Chris Vorster is the director of the Centre for Human Metabolomics at North West University in Potchefstroom.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: In South Africa, round about 150 to 200 babies are born per annum with a lysosomal storage disease.
VO5: These diseases involve a shortage in the enzymes that break down substances in our cells. Symptoms depend on which enzyme is lacking.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: It results in an accumulation of glycogen in the muscle. And that essentially means that all the cardiac, epithelial and smooth muscle in his body doesn't work correctly.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: The symptoms and signs become worse and worse as time goes on and may in a very, very severe way affect their quality of life.
VO6: Most patients with severe Pompe disease die before their second birthday. But Kelly fought for a lifesaving treatment for Juan: enzyme replacement therapy, a synthetic version of the missing enzyme.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: If I could define the future in a droplet, that's what it felt like for us.
UPSOUND: Masa Kekana: Does it bother you at all that you’re going to have to be dependent on this treatment for the rest of your life?
Juan: No. It doesn’t bother me. It’s like a little brother, he won’t leave you alone so you must live with it now.
VO7: The treatment doesn’t cure his disease, but dramatically slows its progression - and has given Juan a normal life.
UPSOUND: Juan du Plessis: I play soccer, cricket and rugby. And a bit of hockey.
Masa: Do you feel like a normal kid?
Juan: Yes, 100% a normal child.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: we're not acutely sick anymore. We have chronic illness, and the critical thing is that he's not a burden to the state. He's not a burden to social services.
VO8: But the treatment is astronomically expensive. One month’s supply costs over R500 000. Medical aid covers the cost for Juan’s infusions. But not everyone is that lucky.
UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: When he learns something new, you're almost like, ok but for how long? How long is he going to be able to do this before it's taken away from him?
VO9: Michaney and Jacques de Wet are parents to busy three year-old Zachary. Last year, Zachary was diagnosed with a lysosomal storage disorder called Hunter Syndrome.
UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: Once we got that diagnosis… [cries] Sorry. It's life changing. To everyone else, he seems healthy. But he's got two leaking heart valves. He's got delays in his development. As a mom, you don't have kids and think, you know, this is going to be your journey.
VO10: Michaney and Jacques are fighting desperately to access enzyme replacement therapy for their son.
UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: We've been jumping through hoops and filling out forms and they just every time just send you this letter with this fancy jargon on it. And basically, at the end of the day, it's just to say no.
VO11: They can’t afford the cost - over R100 000 a month - and without treatment, Zachary’s health is declining.
UPSOUND: Jacques de Wet: If his heart starts deteriorating more, there's nothing you can do. If his cognitive ability starts to deteriorate, and he ends up not knowing how to walk, not knowing how to communicate, not knowing how to eat.
UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: Currently he's looking at a life expectancy of 10 to 20 years, depending on how fast his disease progresses. If he gets his treatment now, he can live to 40, 50 years. I mean, that's worth fighting for.
LINK: One of my own personal dreams is to one day become a mom. And I can’t imagine that dream coming true, then being told my child is suffering from a rare disease, finding out there is treatment for that disease, but I can’t access it.
VO12: Life-threatening lysosomal storage disorders are prescribed minimum benefit conditions - that is, conditions for which all medical aid schemes must generally fund treatment.
UPSOUND: Dr Rajesh Patel: It's not as simple as, it's a PMB, It has to be covered. The regulations allow medical schemes to apply efficacy, evidence based guidelines, health economic guidelines and consider affordability.
VO13: Dr Rajesh Patel is the Head of Health Systems Strengthening at the Board of Healthcare Funders, which represents the majority of South Africa’s private medical schemes.
UPSOUND: Dr Rajesh Patel: There's infinite needs, but there's finite resources and that finite resources need to be managed for servicing everybody out there.
Masa: These are rare diseases. Is it really going to dent them that much?
Dr Patel: It can be. So you've got medical schemes of different sizes…You can't get to a scenario where meeting the one person's need results in that complete plan, say, losing all the money it has. And then you don't have money to pay for any claims for the rest of the population.
VO14: Challenging a medical aid’s decision is an arduous process. First, the scheme’s internal appeal process must be exhausted, then the patient may approach the Council for Medical Schemes. In 2014, Kelly founded Rare Diseases South Africa, which has represented 17 patients with these disorders at the Council.
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: We have never lost a legal challenge. Never. Every single case that has been put forward through the regulator has been awarded in our favour. But sometimes it takes us three years. And in that three years, I mean, last year at the end of last year, we had a case go forward. In the time that we argued that case, the child lost his ability to walk and talk.
UPSOUND: Masa Kekana: It just seems to us that medical aid schemes are very cynical, because they go and appeal these decisions even once patients have won.
Dr Patel: It's very difficult for me to comment on those without seeing the specifics. But to me, it's quite clear, you know, if affordability is your reason for not funding, then demonstrate the volatility on the claims, the impact it would have on the reserves of that fund and on the contributions going into the future. There’s no such a thing that, it’s unaffordable, so you get zero. There is a certain amount that you can contribute towards and that's what they need to determine.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: I’ve quite frequently asked medical aids, where's your analysis on why you can't afford it? But either they’re not sharing this or it doesn't exist. And I'm not picking on any particular medical aid here. I'm referring to every decision maker that denies a child access to life saving therapy without having made absolutely sure that there's no way to afford it.
LINK: The Council for Medical Schemes, which regulates private medical aid schemes in South Africa, refused our invitation for an on-camera interview about why these patients continue to be forced through lengthy hearings and appeal processes just to get access to treatment.
VO15: The regulator even declined to respond to our questions in writing, saying “internal processes” prevented engagement on the matter.
UPSOUND: Masa Kekana: Not being able to get the funding for the treatment that he needs, is that a slow death?
Michaney: And it's a hard death. I can't imagine myself going through it, let alone watching my child go through it.
VO16: Zinolia Bowes knows that heart-breaking journey all too well. Her son Crishendo was diagnosed with Hunter Syndrome when he was two.
UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: He would just sit on the stoop and watch other kids play. He couldn’t live his life to the fullest as a child.
VO17: When Crishendo was 14, Zinolia got a job with a medical aid benefit, and he was approved for a six-month trial on enzyme replacement therapy.
UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: it was like a miracle. We could visibly see changes.
Masa: What kinds of changes?
Zinolia: His hands. He could, he could grip. His breathing improved, his mobility, he had more energy.
VO17: But then Zinolia changed jobs, and her new medical aid was not so sympathetic.
UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: We took the same steps applying for the treatment. Sending them motivation from the doctors. And at this point, he was at an age where he understood exactly what was happening.
VO18: Treatment withdrawn, Zinolia looked on helplessly as the disease accelerated.
UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: He’s now battling to walk from the bathroom to the kitchen…to eat. It was like the same nightmare, but just ten times worse.
VO19: Crishendo was admitted to hospital with heart failure and passed away last year aged just 16.
UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: One of the doctors called and she said, he’s just not responding. And that's when I had to make a decision and decide when to switch off life support.
LINK: Rare diseases affect as many as 400 million people worldwide. But for many of these patients, they’re isolated, poorly understood, and very vulnerable. That should make them the people we work harder to protect, but very often, their stories don’t turn out like that.

PROMOS

PROMO 1: 21 SECONDS
LINK: Imagine learning your child has a rare, life-threatening disease, treatment is available, only for your medical aid not to cover.
UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: As a mom, you don't have kids and think, you know, this is going to be your journey.
UPSOUND: Dr Rajesh Patel: In healthcare, we talk about there's infinite needs, but there's finite resources.

PROMO 2: 21 SECONDS
UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: This stuff is like liquid gold for us. It's like liquid life.
VO: Imagine learning that your child has a rare, life-threatening disease, only to be told that treatment is unaffordable even for your medical aid.
UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: I’ve quite frequently asked medical aids, where's your analysis on why you can't afford it? But either they’re not sharing this, or it doesn't exist.

PROMO 3: 11 SECONDS
LINK: Imagine learning your child has a rare, life-threatening disease. You learn that treatment is available - only for your medical aid not to cover.

Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 10 July 2022 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 13 July 2022 Press Release: Imagine learning your child has a rare, life-threatening, but treatable disease...and it's a condition covered by medical aid...only for your medical aid scheme to refuse funding for lifesaving treatment. This is a story about a group of rare, genetic disorders resulting in a deficiency of the essential enzymes needed to process substances in our cells. The substances build up on organs, bones and muscles, leading to irreversible damage and eventually death. Enzyme Replacement Therapy replaces the deficient enzymes, slowing progression of the disease, increasing life expectancy, and often allowing the patient to live a normal life. But it is stunningly expensive: a single month’s supply can cost hundreds of thousands of rands. The good news for patients is that these diseases are Prescribed Minimum Benefits, which means that according to the Medical Schemes Act, medical aid schemes are obligated to cover treatment. And yet in case after case, medical aids refuse, dragging patients and their families through lengthy hearings with the Council for Medical Schemes. To date, the process has always resulted in a decision in the patient's favour. But patients will suffer permanent disease progression and damage - and in some cases, even death - while they wait. We tell the emotional stories of families on the receiving end of this bitter conundrum as they battle to ensure a healthy future for their children. Script: UPSOUND: Juan du Plessis: Dad’s going to make a silly mistake and now I’m back in the game. LINK: We’re here in Hartbeespoort on an ordinary Sunday, to visit a family as they go about their weekend routine. But ordinary life has not come easily for Kelly du Plessis and her son, Juan. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: So this is just our mixing process. It takes about two and a bit hours. Masa: Two and a half hours! Kelly: Ja. And then it takes another five and a half to 6 hours to actually infuse. So it's quite a commitment. This is our Sunday every second week, except I'm normally in pyjamas. VO1: This is a story about lifesaving medical treatment - but it’s also a story about parents fighting to keep their children alive. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: This medicine keeps his heart functioning. It keeps him breathing. It keeps all of his muscle functioning properly. This stuff is like liquid gold for us. It's like liquid life. VO2: Juan was very young when Kelly realised he was facing serious health problems. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: I think I knew from about the time he was ten days old, was the first time he had a significant choking episode. Other children were a lot more active than he was, and they were definitively reaching their gross motor milestones easier. VO3: By the time Juan was 11 months old, he had a diagnosis. He has Pompe disease, one of a group of rare genetic diseases called lysosomal storage disorders. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: If you combine them, they have an incidence of around about one in 5000 to 1 in 6000 live births. VO4: Professor Chris Vorster is the director of the Centre for Human Metabolomics at North West University in Potchefstroom. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: In South Africa, round about 150 to 200 babies are born per annum with a lysosomal storage disease. VO5: These diseases involve a shortage in the enzymes that break down substances in our cells. Symptoms depend on which enzyme is lacking. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: It results in an accumulation of glycogen in the muscle. And that essentially means that all the cardiac, epithelial and smooth muscle in his body doesn't work correctly. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: The symptoms and signs become worse and worse as time goes on and may in a very, very severe way affect their quality of life. VO6: Most patients with severe Pompe disease die before their second birthday. But Kelly fought for a lifesaving treatment for Juan: enzyme replacement therapy, a synthetic version of the missing enzyme. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: If I could define the future in a droplet, that's what it felt like for us. UPSOUND: Masa Kekana: Does it bother you at all that you’re going to have to be dependent on this treatment for the rest of your life? Juan: No. It doesn’t bother me. It’s like a little brother, he won’t leave you alone so you must live with it now. VO7: The treatment doesn’t cure his disease, but dramatically slows its progression - and has given Juan a normal life. UPSOUND: Juan du Plessis: I play soccer, cricket and rugby. And a bit of hockey. Masa: Do you feel like a normal kid? Juan: Yes, 100% a normal child. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: we're not acutely sick anymore. We have chronic illness, and the critical thing is that he's not a burden to the state. He's not a burden to social services. VO8: But the treatment is astronomically expensive. One month’s supply costs over R500 000. Medical aid covers the cost for Juan’s infusions. But not everyone is that lucky. UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: When he learns something new, you're almost like, ok but for how long? How long is he going to be able to do this before it's taken away from him? VO9: Michaney and Jacques de Wet are parents to busy three year-old Zachary. Last year, Zachary was diagnosed with a lysosomal storage disorder called Hunter Syndrome. UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: Once we got that diagnosis… [cries] Sorry. It's life changing. To everyone else, he seems healthy. But he's got two leaking heart valves. He's got delays in his development. As a mom, you don't have kids and think, you know, this is going to be your journey. VO10: Michaney and Jacques are fighting desperately to access enzyme replacement therapy for their son. UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: We've been jumping through hoops and filling out forms and they just every time just send you this letter with this fancy jargon on it. And basically, at the end of the day, it's just to say no. VO11: They can’t afford the cost - over R100 000 a month - and without treatment, Zachary’s health is declining. UPSOUND: Jacques de Wet: If his heart starts deteriorating more, there's nothing you can do. If his cognitive ability starts to deteriorate, and he ends up not knowing how to walk, not knowing how to communicate, not knowing how to eat. UPSOUND: Michaney de Wet: Currently he's looking at a life expectancy of 10 to 20 years, depending on how fast his disease progresses. If he gets his treatment now, he can live to 40, 50 years. I mean, that's worth fighting for. LINK: One of my own personal dreams is to one day become a mom. And I can’t imagine that dream coming true, then being told my child is suffering from a rare disease, finding out there is treatment for that disease, but I can’t access it. VO12: Life-threatening lysosomal storage disorders are prescribed minimum benefit conditions - that is, conditions for which all medical aid schemes must generally fund treatment. UPSOUND: Dr Rajesh Patel: It's not as simple as, it's a PMB, It has to be covered. The regulations allow medical schemes to apply efficacy, evidence based guidelines, health economic guidelines and consider affordability. VO13: Dr Rajesh Patel is the Head of Health Systems Strengthening at the Board of Healthcare Funders, which represents the majority of South Africa’s private medical schemes. UPSOUND: Dr Rajesh Patel: There's infinite needs, but there's finite resources and that finite resources need to be managed for servicing everybody out there. Masa: These are rare diseases. Is it really going to dent them that much? Dr Patel: It can be. So you've got medical schemes of different sizes…You can't get to a scenario where meeting the one person's need results in that complete plan, say, losing all the money it has. And then you don't have money to pay for any claims for the rest of the population. VO14: Challenging a medical aid’s decision is an arduous process. First, the scheme’s internal appeal process must be exhausted, then the patient may approach the Council for Medical Schemes. In 2014, Kelly founded Rare Diseases South Africa, which has represented 17 patients with these disorders at the Council. UPSOUND: Kelly du Plessis: We have never lost a legal challenge. Never. Every single case that has been put forward through the regulator has been awarded in our favour. But sometimes it takes us three years. And in that three years, I mean, last year at the end of last year, we had a case go forward. In the time that we argued that case, the child lost his ability to walk and talk. UPSOUND: Masa Kekana: It just seems to us that medical aid schemes are very cynical, because they go and appeal these decisions even once patients have won. Dr Patel: It's very difficult for me to comment on those without seeing the specifics. But to me, it's quite clear, you know, if affordability is your reason for not funding, then demonstrate the volatility on the claims, the impact it would have on the reserves of that fund and on the contributions going into the future. There’s no such a thing that, it’s unaffordable, so you get zero. There is a certain amount that you can contribute towards and that's what they need to determine. UPSOUND: Prof Chris Vorster: I’ve quite frequently asked medical aids, where's your analysis on why you can't afford it? But either they’re not sharing this or it doesn't exist. And I'm not picking on any particular medical aid here. I'm referring to every decision maker that denies a child access to life saving therapy without having made absolutely sure that there's no way to afford it. LINK: The Council for Medical Schemes, which regulates private medical aid schemes in South Africa, refused our invitation for an on-camera interview about why these patients continue to be forced through lengthy hearings and appeal processes just to get access to treatment. VO15: The regulator even declined to respond to our questions in writing, saying “internal processes” prevented engagement on the matter. UPSOUND: Masa Kekana: Not being able to get the funding for the treatment that he needs, is that a slow death? Michaney: And it's a hard death. I can't imagine myself going through it, let alone watching my child go through it. VO16: Zinolia Bowes knows that heart-breaking journey all too well. Her son Crishendo was diagnosed with Hunter Syndrome when he was two. UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: He would just sit on the stoop and watch other kids play. He couldn’t live his life to the fullest as a child. VO17: When Crishendo was 14, Zinolia got a job with a medical aid benefit, and he was approved for a six-month trial on enzyme replacement therapy. UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: it was like a miracle. We could visibly see changes. Masa: What kinds of changes? Zinolia: His hands. He could, he could grip. His breathing improved, his mobility, he had more energy. VO17: But then Zinolia changed jobs, and her new medical aid was not so sympathetic. UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: We took the same steps applying for the treatment. Sending them motivation from the doctors. And at this point, he was at an age where he understood exactly what was happening. VO18: Treatment withdrawn, Zinolia looked on helplessly as the disease accelerated. UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: He’s now battling to walk from the bathroom to the kitchen…to eat. It was like the same nightmare, but just ten times worse. VO19: Crishendo was admitted to hospital with heart failure and passed away last year aged just 16. UPSOUND: Zinolia Bowes: One of the doctors called and she said, he’s just not responding. And that's when I had to make a decision and decide when to switch off life support. LINK: Rare diseases affect as many as 400 million people worldwide. But for many of these patients, they’re isolated, poorly understood, and very vulnerable. That should make them the people we work harder to protect, but very often, their stories don’t turn out like that. metadata.Unique Selling Point: Enzyme therapy is a new and stunningly expensive treatment for a small group of diseases that affect only a few people in the world. Treatment can cost hundreds of thousands per month - yet it is the only thing that can offer these people a chance at a normal life. And these diseases are Prescribed Minimum Benefits under the Medical Schemes Act, which means that medical aid schemes are obligated to cover the treatment. And yet in case after case, medical aids refuse, dragging patients and their families through lengthy hearings with the CMS which to date, have always resulted in a decision in the patient's favour. But patients will suffer permanent disease progression and damage - and in some cases, even death, while they wait.
metadata.Summary: Rare diseases affect 4% of the world's population: cumulatively, a huge number of people. This is a story about a group of rare, genetic, metabolic diseases affecting around 90 known patients in South Africa. These diseases result in a deficiency of enzymes needed to process carbohydrates, proteins and fats, resulting in a build-up on organs, joints and muscles, leading to irreversible damage and eventually death. Life expectancy differs according to the type and severity of the disease, but is severely curtailed. Many children aren't diagnosed until damage has occurred, thanks to the diseases' rarity. For those lucky enough to get an early diagnosis, the good news is that it's possible in some conditions to replace the deficient enzymes, which slows progression of the disease, increases life expectancy and allows the child to live normally. Even better: "Life-threatening congenital abnormalities of carbohydrate, lipid, protein and amino acid metabolism" appear on the list of Prescribed Minimum Benefits for which medical aids (and government) must provide treatment. The treatment is "medical management": the only available and effective version is enzyme replacement therapy. But that's where the good news ends. Medical aid schemes refuse to approve the treatment, citing its "biological" or "experimental" nature, claiming they can't afford it, or saying the disease is not a PMB. Parents are forced to watch their child deteriorate, eventually being placed on a ventilator or hospitalised (for which medical aid pays) and dying. Enter Rare Diseases South Africa. They've taken numerous schemes repeatedly to the Council for Medical Schemes and haven't lost a single case, forcing medical aid schemes to pay for treatment. And yet every new patient is forced to go through the same painful process, waiting up to three years and facing irreversible deterioration.
metadata.Further information: Rare Diseases South Africa was founded by Kelly du Plessis, whose son Juan was fortuitously diagnosed with Pompe Disease at only 11 months. Most babies with Pompe don't live to see their second birthdays. Juan was the first South African child to receive enzyme replacement therapy covered by his medical aid, thanks to Kelly's fight for coverage. Today he is an energetic 13 year-old with completely normal cardiac function, thanks to his treatment of 12 years. He is the success story for enzyme replacement therapy - but sadly too few children will have the same chance. Having won her own battle, Kelly was inspired to fight for other families, and today Rare Diseases South Africa advocates for every patient with a rare disease free of charge. They have taken numerous cases of metabolic storage disorders to the CMS and have never lost. Despite creating a precedent for the coverage of these diseases by medical aid schemes, however, they continue to see many children delayed and permanently damaged thanks to the schemes' refusal. OTHER CASE STUDIES Zachary de Wet is a three year old with a shock of blond hair and a sweet smile. He was fortunately diagnosed with Mucopolysaccharidosis type II when he was about two years old, thanks to an alert doctor who recognised some of the symptoms. MPSII is the deficiency of a protein required to metabolise proteins, and these proteins then build up all over Zachary's body, including on his heart and other organs, his joints and his muscles. They can also cross the blood-brain barrier. Once a seemingly normal toddler, Zachary now shows some developmental delays in his speech and cognition, and two valves in his heart have started leaking. Although his family is on a medical aid, the scheme (MediHelp) has refused to pay for treatment. Facing the prospect of a long battle during which Zachary may lose his ability to walk and face permanent mental disability, the family has decided to take the scheme to court, hoping to set a legal precedent for other families. Crishendo Bowers was a sweet, funny kid with a big smile, and MPSII. He received treatment for several years until his granny, who used to pay for his medical aid, passed away. Although his mom quickly found a job which included medical aid, the new scheme (Bankmed) refused to pay for his life-saving treatment. After a year-long battle, Crishendo passed away in 2021 from complications of the disease without ever receiving approval. Mbali Mvubelo is a young woman who was diagnosed with Gaucher disease many years ago. She had a spleen so large that she was continuously shamed for being a pregnant teenager. She now receives treatment at Charlotte Maxeke hospital and is living a normal life now despite her condition. She has a disease for which treatment is fairly available in government, but others who have different forms of metabolic disease are less fortunate.
